## Definition

Assume countable choice, fix an integer $d\geq1$, and use the Euclidean norm $\|x\|_2=\sqrt{\langle x,x\rangle}$ from [[def-euclidean-inner-product]] and the $d$-dimensional Lebesgue measure $\lambda_d$ from [[def-lebesgue-measure-and-the-lebesgue-sigma-algebra]]. Countable choice ensures the stated Lebesgue set function is a measure and every Borel set is Lebesgue measurable ([[def-countable-choice]], [[thm-borel-sets-are-lebesgue-measurable]]). For $S\subseteq\mathbb R^d$, define $\operatorname{dist}_2(x,S)=\inf_{y\in S}\|x-y\|_2$, with $\operatorname{dist}_2(x,\varnothing)=+\infty$. The topological boundary of $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^d$ is
$$\partial\Omega=\{x\in\mathbb R^d:\text{every }\epsilon>0\text{ has }B_\epsilon(x)\cap\Omega\ne\varnothing\text{ and }B_\epsilon(x)\setminus\Omega\ne\varnothing\},\qquad B_\epsilon(x)=\{y:\|y-x\|_2<\epsilon\}.$$
For a Lebesgue-measurable set $A$, write $|A|=\lambda_d(A)$. For a bounded set $\Omega$ and $R>0$, define its two-sided boundary layer
$$\partial_R\Omega=\{x\in\mathbb R^d:\operatorname{dist}_2(x,\partial\Omega)\leq R\},$$
where $\operatorname{dist}_2$ is the Euclidean distance just defined. A van Hove sequence is a sequence of bounded Lebesgue-measurable sets $(\Omega_k)_{k\in\mathbb N}$ with $0<|\Omega_k|<\infty$, $|\Omega_k|\to\infty$, and
$$\frac{|\partial_R\Omega_k|}{|\Omega_k|}\longrightarrow0\qquad\text{for every fixed }R>0.$$
The boundary is closed, distance to a nonempty set is continuous, and for bounded $\Omega$ its $R$-neighborhood is bounded; hence each $\partial_R\Omega$ is Borel and has finite Lebesgue measure ([[prop-lebesgue-measure-is-sigma-finite-and-finite-on-bounded-sets]]).
The condition controls both inner and outer boundary neighborhoods. It does not impose connectedness, a bounded aspect ratio, smooth boundaries, or a periodic identification.

## Definition

Assume AC. Fix an integer dimension $d\geq1$, use the Euclidean norm $|\cdot|_2$ from [[def-euclidean-inner-product]], define $|x|_\infty=\max_j|x_j|$, and use the numerical coordinate conventions in [[def-tdmath-poisson-configuration-reference]]. A finite configuration is a finite subset $\omega\subset\mathbb R^d$ with no repeated points; its number of points is $N(\omega)$. A pair potential is an even Borel function, measurable for the Borel sigma-algebra generated by open sets ([[def-borel-sigma-algebra]]), $\phi:\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R\cup\{+\infty\}$, where even means $\phi(-x)=\phi(x)$. Define
$$H_\phi(\omega)=\sum_{\{x,y\}\subset\omega}\phi(x-y),\qquad H_\phi(\varnothing)=0.$$
The sum is over unordered two-point subsets, so every term is evaluated at a nonzero separation; if any term is $+\infty$, the sum is $+\infty$.

The potential is stable if some $B\geq0$ satisfies $H_\phi(\omega)\geq-BN(\omega)$ for every finite configuration. It is superstable in the Georgii splitting convention if $\phi=\phi_s+\phi_r$, where $\phi_s$ is stable and $\phi_r\geq0$ everywhere and, for some $r_0,\delta>0$, $\phi_r(x)\geq\delta$ whenever $|x|_\infty\leq r_0$. It is lower regular if a nonnegative nonincreasing $\psi:[0,\infty)\to[0,+\infty]$ satisfies
$$\phi(x)\geq-\psi(|x|_\infty),\qquad \int_0^\infty\psi(r)r^{d-1}\,dr<\infty.$$
It is regular if it is lower regular and, for some $R<\infty$, $\phi(x)\leq\psi(|x|_\infty)$ whenever $|x|_\infty\geq R$. These are the conventions used for the interacting results on this page. A genuine divergent positive core is the separate additional condition that some nonincreasing $\chi:(0,r_1]\to(0,\infty)$ satisfies $\phi(x)\geq\chi(|x|_\infty)$ for $0<|x|_\infty\leq r_1$ and $\int_0^{r_1}\chi(r)r^{d-1}dr=+\infty$; it is not implied by superstability.

For $L>0$ put $\Lambda_L=[0,L)^d$, $V_L=L^d$, and let $H_{L,\mathrm{free}}$ be $H_\phi$ for configurations restricted to $\Lambda_L$. For a regular potential and sufficiently large periodic cubes, periodize $\omega\subset\Lambda_L$ by $\omega^{\mathrm{per}}=\{x+Lk:x\in\omega,\ k\in\mathbb Z^d\}$ and set
$$H_{L,\mathrm{per}}(\omega)=\frac12\sum_{x\in\omega}\sum_{y\in\omega^{\mathrm{per}},\ y\ne x}\phi(y-x),$$
interpreting the value as $+\infty$ if a positive infinite term occurs. Under this regularity hypothesis, the far image sum is absolutely convergent for all sufficiently large $L$ by [[lem-tdmath-integrable-tail-diagonal-gap]]; this is the image convention used below. With fixed numerical length and energy units, the canonical positional partition is
$$Z(L,N;\beta)=\frac1{N!}\int_{\Lambda_L^N}e^{-\beta H_\phi(q_1,\ldots,q_N)}dq_1\cdots dq_N,\quad Z(L,0;\beta)=1,$$
where the tuple notation means $H_\phi(q_1,\ldots,q_N):=H_\phi(\{q_1,\ldots,q_N\})$ when the coordinates are distinct, and $H_\phi(q_1,\ldots,q_N):=+\infty$ on collision diagonals. The integrand is therefore zero on collisions; these diagonals have product Lebesgue measure zero by the no-collision construction in [[def-tdmath-poisson-configuration-reference]], so this convention leaves all partition integrals unchanged. For $N=0$ the empty tuple has energy zero. Here $\beta>0$, and the grand partition is $\Xi(L;a,\beta)=\sum_{N\geq0}a^NZ(L,N;\beta)$ for numerical activity $a>0$. The normalized unit-intensity Poisson version is $Z_Q(L;z,\beta)=E_{Q_{\Lambda_L}}[z^{N_{\Lambda_L}}e^{-\beta H_{L,\mathrm{free}}}]$; since the Poisson density contributes $e^{-V_L}$, $\Xi(L;z,\beta)=e^{V_L}Z_Q(L;z,\beta)$. A physical pressure identification is not part of this mathematical definition.

For a probability law $P$ on the configuration space of [[def-tdmath-poisson-configuration-reference]], stationarity means $P\circ T_x^{-1}=P$ for every $x\in\mathbb R^d$. When $P$ is stationary and $E_PN_{[0,1)^d}<\infty$ (finite intensity), write $\rho(P)=E_PN_{[0,1)^d}$. Use the finite-region relative entropy $D$ defined in [[def-tdmath-finite-region-relative-entropy]]. If $\phi$ is stable with constant $B$, then $H_{L,\mathrm{free}}\geq-BN_{\Lambda_L}$, so the negative part of $H_{L,\mathrm{free}}$ is $P$-integrable for every such $P$. Whenever the limit exists, write
$$\mathcal E(P)=\lim_{L\to\infty}V_L^{-1}E_PH_{L,\mathrm{free}},\qquad I(P)=\lim_{L\to\infty}V_L^{-1}D(P_{\Lambda_L}\Vert Q_{\Lambda_L}).$$
In the variational results below, $\Phi(P)$ denotes this same positional energy density: $\Phi(P):=\mathcal E(P)$. The cited results establish existence under their stated hypotheses; this definition does not assume either limit exists for every stationary finite-intensity law.

Fix an integer dimension $d\geq1$, use the Euclidean norm $|\cdot|_2$ from [[def-euclidean-inner-product]], define $|x|_\infty=\max_j|x_j|$, and use the numerical coordinate conventions in [[def-tdmath-poisson-configuration-reference]]. A finite configuration is a finite subset $\omega\subset\mathbb R^d$ with no repeated points; its number of points is $N(\omega)$. A pair potential is an even Borel function, measurable for the Borel sigma-algebra generated by open sets ([[def-borel-sigma-algebra]]), $\phi:\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R\cup\{+\infty\}$, where even means $\phi(-x)=\phi(x)$. Define
$$H_\phi(\omega)=\sum_{\{x,y\}\subset\omega}\phi(x-y),\qquad H_\phi(\varnothing)=0.$$
The sum is over unordered two-point subsets, so every term is evaluated at a nonzero separation; if any term is $+\infty$, the sum is $+\infty$.

The potential is stable if some $B\geq0$ satisfies $H_\phi(\omega)\geq-BN(\omega)$ for every finite configuration. It is superstable in the Georgii splitting convention if $\phi=\phi_s+\phi_r$, where $\phi_s$ is stable and $\phi_r\geq0$ everywhere and, for some $r_0,\delta>0$, $\phi_r(x)\geq\delta$ whenever $|x|_\infty\leq r_0$. It is lower regular if a nonnegative nonincreasing $\psi:[0,\infty)\to[0,+\infty]$ satisfies
$$\phi(x)\geq-\psi(|x|_\infty),\qquad \int_0^\infty\psi(r)r^{d-1}\,dr<\infty.$$
It is regular if it is lower regular and, for some $R<\infty$, $\phi(x)\leq\psi(|x|_\infty)$ whenever $|x|_\infty\geq R$. These are the conventions used for the interacting results on this page. A genuine divergent positive core is the separate additional condition that some nonincreasing $\chi:(0,r_1]\to(0,\infty)$ satisfies $\phi(x)\geq\chi(|x|_\infty)$ for $0<|x|_\infty\leq r_1$ and $\int_0^{r_1}\chi(r)r^{d-1}dr=+\infty$; it is not implied by superstability.

For $L>0$ put $\Lambda_L=[0,L)^d$, $V_L=L^d$, and let $H_{L,\mathrm{free}}$ be $H_\phi$ for configurations restricted to $\Lambda_L$. For a regular potential and sufficiently large periodic cubes, periodize $\omega\subset\Lambda_L$ by $\omega^{\mathrm{per}}=\{x+Lk:x\in\omega,\ k\in\mathbb Z^d\}$ and set
$$H_{L,\mathrm{per}}(\omega)=\frac12\sum_{x\in\omega}\sum_{y\in\omega^{\mathrm{per}},\ y\ne x}\phi(y-x),$$
interpreting the value as $+\infty$ if a positive infinite term occurs. Under this regularity hypothesis, the far image sum is absolutely convergent for all sufficiently large $L$ by [[lem-tdmath-integrable-tail-diagonal-gap]]; this is the image convention used below. With fixed numerical length and energy units, the canonical positional partition is
$$Z(L,N;\beta)=\frac1{N!}\int_{\Lambda_L^N}e^{-\beta H_\phi(q_1,\ldots,q_N)}dq_1\cdots dq_N,\quad Z(L,0;\beta)=1,$$
where the tuple notation means $H_\phi(q_1,\ldots,q_N):=H_\phi(\{q_1,\ldots,q_N\})$ when the coordinates are distinct, and $H_\phi(q_1,\ldots,q_N):=+\infty$ on collision diagonals. The integrand is therefore zero on collisions; these diagonals have product Lebesgue measure zero by the no-collision construction in [[def-tdmath-poisson-configuration-reference]], so this convention leaves all partition integrals unchanged. For $N=0$ the empty tuple has energy zero. Here $\beta>0$, and the grand partition is $\Xi(L;a,\beta)=\sum_{N\geq0}a^NZ(L,N;\beta)$ for numerical activity $a>0$. The normalized unit-intensity Poisson version is $Z_Q(L;z,\beta)=E_{Q_{\Lambda_L}}[z^{N_{\Lambda_L}}e^{-\beta H_{L,\mathrm{free}}}]$; since the Poisson density contributes $e^{-V_L}$, $\Xi(L;z,\beta)=e^{V_L}Z_Q(L;z,\beta)$. A physical pressure identification is not part of this mathematical definition.

For a probability law $P$ on the configuration space of [[def-tdmath-poisson-configuration-reference]], stationarity means $P\circ T_x^{-1}=P$ for every $x\in\mathbb R^d$. When $P$ is stationary and $E_PN_{[0,1)^d}<\infty$ (finite intensity), write $\rho(P)=E_PN_{[0,1)^d}$. Use the finite-region relative entropy $D$ defined in [[def-tdmath-finite-region-relative-entropy]]. If $\phi$ is stable with constant $B$, then $H_{L,\mathrm{free}}\geq-BN_{\Lambda_L}$, so the negative part of $H_{L,\mathrm{free}}$ is $P$-integrable for every such $P$. Whenever the limit exists, write
$$\mathcal E(P)=\lim_{L\to\infty}V_L^{-1}E_PH_{L,\mathrm{free}},\qquad I(P)=\lim_{L\to\infty}V_L^{-1}D(P_{\Lambda_L}\Vert Q_{\Lambda_L}).$$
In the variational results below, $\Phi(P)$ denotes this same positional energy density: $\Phi(P):=\mathcal E(P)$. The cited results establish existence under their stated hypotheses; this definition does not assume either limit exists for every stationary finite-intensity law.

## Definition

Use the cube $\Lambda_L=[0,L)^d$ and the translation $T_x$ defined in [[def-tdmath-poisson-configuration-reference]]. For a finite configuration $\omega\subset\Lambda_L$, let $\omega^{(L)}=\{q+Lk:q\in\omega,\ k\in\mathbb Z^d\}$ be its periodic continuation. Define its **periodized empirical field**
$$R_{L,\omega}:=\frac1{L^d}\int_{\Lambda_L}\delta_{T_x\omega^{(L)}}\,dx.$$
The integral is the push-forward of normalized Lebesgue measure on $\Lambda_L$ under $x\mapsto T_x\omega^{(L)}$. For any probability law $C_L$ on finite configurations in $\Lambda_L$, define its **empirical-field barycenter** as the probability mixture
$$\bar C_L(B)=\int C_L(d\omega)R_{L,\omega}(B)$$
for every measurable configuration event $B$. By [[thm-tonelli-theorem-for-sigma-finite-product-spaces]], for a nonnegative measurable test $f$, the mixture identity holds with values in $[0,+\infty]$. For a signed local tame $f$ from [[def-tdmath-local-tame-topology]], the finite expectation formula
$$\bar C_L(f)=\int C_L(d\omega)R_{L,\omega}(f)=\frac1{L^d}\int_{\Lambda_L}E_{C_L}[f(T_x\omega^{(L)})]\,dx$$
is asserted when $\int C_L(d\omega)R_{L,\omega}(|f|)<\infty$. In particular $E_{C_L}N<\infty$ suffices: if a bounded support $A$ is contained in a box of side $a$, then $N_A(T_x\omega^{(L)})\leq (\lceil a/L\rceil+2)^dN(\omega)$ uniformly in $x$. The growth bound $|f|\leq b(1+N_A)$ therefore gives absolute integrability. For stationary laws write $\rho(P)=E_PN_{[0,1)^d}\in[0,+\infty]$, with finite intensity meaning $\rho(P)<\infty$; this agrees with the finite-intensity convention in [[def-tdmath-superstable-regular-interaction]]. This is a spatial average over the finite box, not the raw finite-volume law viewed at a fixed origin.

The integrand is therefore zero on collisions; these diagonals have product Lebesgue measure zero by the no-collision construction in [[def-tdmath-poisson-configuration-reference]], so this convention leaves all partition integrals unchanged. For $N=0$ the empty tuple has energy zero. Here $\beta>0$, and the grand partition is $\Xi(L;a,\beta)=\sum_{N\geq0}a^NZ(L,N;\beta)$ for numerical activity $a>0$. The normalized unit-intensity Poisson version is $Z_Q(L;z,\beta)=E_{Q_{\Lambda_L}}[z^{N_{\Lambda_L}}e^{-\beta H_{L,\mathrm{free}}}]$; since the Poisson density contributes $e^{-V_L}$, $\Xi(L;z,\beta)=e^{V_L}Z_Q(L;z,\beta)$. A physical pressure identification is not part of this mathematical definition.

For a probability law $P$ on the configuration space of [[def-tdmath-poisson-configuration-reference]], stationarity means $P\circ T_x^{-1}=P$ for every $x\in\mathbb R^d$. When $P$ is stationary and $E_PN_{[0,1)^d}<\infty$ (finite intensity), write $\rho(P)=E_PN_{[0,1)^d}$. Use the finite-region relative entropy $D$ defined in [[def-tdmath-finite-region-relative-entropy]]. If $\phi$ is stable with constant $B$, then $H_{L,\mathrm{free}}\geq-BN_{\Lambda_L}$, so the negative part of $H_{L,\mathrm{free}}$ is $P$-integrable for every such $P$. Whenever the limit exists, write
$$\mathcal E(P)=\lim_{L\to\infty}V_L^{-1}E_PH_{L,\mathrm{free}},\qquad I(P)=\lim_{L\to\infty}V_L^{-1}D(P_{\Lambda_L}\Vert Q_{\Lambda_L}).$$
In the variational results below, $\Phi(P)$ denotes this same positional energy density: $\Phi(P):=\mathcal E(P)$. The cited results establish existence under their stated hypotheses; this definition does not assume either limit exists for every stationary finite-intensity law.

derivations.claim: Since $\psi$ is nonincreasing, $0\leq g^d\psi(g)\leq \frac{d}{1-2^{-d}}\int_{g/2}^{g}r^{d-1}\psi(r)dr$ for $g>2R_0$: on $[g/2,g]$, $\psi(r)\geq\psi(g)$, and integration of $r^{d-1}$ gives the displayed coefficient. Both the interval integral and the tail integral in $\eta(g)$ tend to zero as $g\to\infty$, so $\eta(g)\to0$.

For $m\geq2$ and $r\in[(m-1)g,mg]$, monotonicity gives $\psi(r)\geq\psi(mg)$ and $r^{d-1}\geq((m-1)g)^{d-1}$. Hence $$ \int_{(m-1)g}^{mg}r^{d-1}\psi(r)dr\geq g^d(m-1)^{d-1}\psi(mg). $$ Since $m^{d-1}\leq2^{d-1}(m-1)^{d-1}$, summing over disjoint intervals yields $\sum_{m\geq2}m^{d-1}\psi(mg)\leq2^{d-1}g^{-d}\int_g^\infty r^{d-1}\psi(r)dr$. The $m=1$ term equals $g^{-d}g^d\psi(g)$, so adding it proves the stated bound because $2^{d-1}\geq1$.

For integer $m\geq\lceil R_0+3\rceil$, monotonicity gives $\psi(r)\geq\psi(m-1)$ on $[m-2,m-1]$, so $\int_{m-2}^{m-1}r^{d-1}\psi(r)dr\geq(m-2)^{d-1}\psi(m-1)$. Since $m^{d-1}\leq c_d(m-2)^{d-1}$ for these $m$, summing over disjoint unit intervals proves $\sum_{m\geq\lceil R_0+3\rceil} m^{d-1}\psi(m-1)<\infty$.

For each integer $k\geq1$, let $G_k$ be the least integer greater than $2R_0$ such that $\eta(g)\leq k^{-2d}$ for every $g\geq G_k$; it exists by step 1.1 and the well-ordering of the positive integers. Choose a strictly increasing sequence $L_k$ with $L_k\geq kG_k$ and $L_k\geq k^2$. For $\ell\geq L_1$, let $k(\ell)=\max\{k:L_k\leq\ell\}$ and $g(\ell)=\ell/k(\ell)$. Then $k(\ell)\to\infty$, $g(\ell)\geq G_{k(\ell)}$ and $g(\ell)\geq k(\ell)$, while $g(\ell)/\ell=1/k(\ell)$. Therefore $$ \left(\frac{\ell}{g(\ell)}\right)^d\eta(g(\ell))\leq k(\ell)^d k(\ell)^{-2d}=k(\ell)^{-d}\to0. $$ This gives all three gap limits.

Fix distinct points $x,y$ in a finite configuration and a period $L>0$. For $|k|_\infty$ larger than $2|x-y|_\infty/L+2R_0/L$, the triangle inequality gives $|x-y+Lk|_\infty\geq L|k|_\infty/2>2R_0$. Grouping lattice indices by $m=|k|_\infty$ and applying the sum bound of step 1.2 with gap $g=L/2$ shows $\sum_k|\phi(x-y+Lk)|<\infty$ whenever $L/2>2R_0$. There are finitely many remaining images; any $+\infty$ term makes the periodic energy $+\infty$ by definition, while otherwise their finite sum is well-defined. This proves the periodic-image convention used in [[def-tdmath-superstable-regular-interaction]] for all sufficiently large $L$.

## Statement

Let $d\geq1$ and let $\phi$ be a regular potential with a nonnegative nonincreasing envelope $\psi:[R_0,\infty)\to[0,\infty)$, where $R_0<\infty$ and $\int_{R_0}^\infty r^{d-1}\psi(r)dr<\infty$. Thus $|\phi(x)|\leq\psi(|x|_\infty)$ for $|x|_\infty\geq R_0$. For $g>2R_0$ set
$$\eta(g)=g^d\psi(g)+\int_g^\infty r^{d-1}\psi(r)dr.$$
Then $\eta(g)\to0$ and
$$\sum_{m=1}^\infty m^{d-1}\psi(mg)\leq 2^{d-1}g^{-d}\eta(g).$$
Moreover, there is a choice $g(\ell)>0$, for all sufficiently large real $\ell$, such that $g(\ell)\to\infty$, $g(\ell)/\ell\to0$, and
$$\left(\frac{\ell}{g(\ell)}\right)^d\eta(g(\ell))\longrightarrow0.$$
For every fixed finite configuration and all sufficiently large periods $L$, the noncoincident periodic-image tail $\sum_{k\in\mathbb Z^d,\ |k|_\infty\geq K_0}|\phi(x-y+Lk)|$ is absolutely convergent. The tail of the cell envelope $\psi(|j|_\infty-1)$ over all sufficiently large integer offsets is summable. This lemma is a deterministic tail estimate; it uses no superstability or thermodynamic-limit conclusion.

boundaries.evidence: Statement the chosen tail gap is positive and tends to infinity, and g>2R_0 is used only in its tail regime. No estimate divides by a zero gap; an empty block contributes zero without division by its count.

citations.quote: It is superstable in the Georgii splitting convention if $\phi=\phi_s+\phi_r$, where $\phi_s$ is stable and $\phi_r\geq0$ everywhere and, for some $r_0,\delta>0$, $\phi_r(x)\geq\delta$ whenever $|x|_\infty\leq r_0$.

derivations.claim:
Choose an integer $k\geq1$ with $1/k\leq r_0$. Partition each unit cell $C_i$ into $k^d$ half-open subcubes of side $1/k$, and denote their occupancies by $n_{i,j}$, $1\leq j\leq k^d$. Distinct points in one subcube have $|x-y|_\infty<1/k\leq r_0$, so their repulsive pair energy is at least $\delta$. Therefore
$$H_{\phi_r}(\omega)\geq\frac{\delta}{2}\sum_{i,j}n_{i,j}(n_{i,j}-1).$$
Writing $\bar n=N_{C_i}(\omega)/k^d$, nonnegativity of $\sum_j(n_{i,j}-\bar n)^2$ expands to $\sum_j n_{i,j}^2\geq N_{C_i}(\omega)^2/k^d$, and $\sum_{i,j}n_{i,j}=N(\omega)$. Thus $H_{\phi_r}(\omega)\geq\frac{\delta}{2k^d}\sum_iN_{C_i}^2-\frac\delta2N$.

The stable part obeys $H_{\phi_s}(\omega)\geq-B_sN$. Add this inequality to step 1.1 and take $A=\delta/(2k^d)$ and $B=B_s+\delta/2$. This proves the cell-quadratic bound. If any term is $+\infty$, the inequality holds in the extended order; otherwise all sums are finite.

Let $\phi=\phi_s+\phi_r$ be superstable in the splitting convention of [[def-tdmath-superstable-regular-interaction]]. Suppose $H_{\phi_s}(\omega)\geq-B_sN(\omega)$ and $\phi_r(x)\geq\delta>0$ for $|x|_\infty\leq r_0$, with $\phi_r\geq0$ elsewhere. For the unit cells $C_i=i+[0,1)^d$, there are constants $A>0$ and $B\geq0$ such that every finite configuration satisfies
$$H_\phi(\omega)\geq A\sum_{i\in\mathbb Z^d}N_{C_i}(\omega)^2-BN(\omega).$$
Only finitely many summands are nonzero. This is the cell form used in the continuum pressure arguments.

Use the cube $\Lambda_L=[0,L)^d$ and the translation $T_x$ defined in [[def-tdmath-poisson-configuration-reference]]. For a finite configuration $\omega\subset\Lambda_L$, let $\omega^{(L)}=\{q+Lk:q\in\omega,\ k\in\mathbb Z^d\}$ be its periodic continuation. Define its **periodized empirical field**
$$R_{L,\omega}:=\frac1{L^d}\int_{\Lambda_L}\delta_{T_x\omega^{(L)}}\,dx.$$
The integral is the push-forward of normalized Lebesgue measure on $\Lambda_L$ under $x\mapsto T_x\omega^{(L)}$. For any probability law $C_L$ on finite configurations in $\Lambda_L$, define its **empirical-field barycenter** as the probability mixture
$$\bar C_L(B)=\int C_L(d\omega)R_{L,\omega}(B)$$
for every measurable configuration event $B$. By [[thm-tonelli-theorem-for-sigma-finite-product-spaces]], for a nonnegative measurable test $f$, the mixture identity holds with values in $[0,+\infty]$. For a signed local tame $f$ from [[def-tdmath-local-tame-topology]], the finite expectation formula
$$\bar C_L(f)=\int C_L(d\omega)R_{L,\omega}(f)=\frac1{L^d}\int_{\Lambda_L}E_{C_L}[f(T_x\omega^{(L)})]\,dx$$
is asserted when $\int C_L(d\omega)R_{L,\omega}(|f|)<\infty$. In particular $E_{C_L}N<\infty$ suffices: if a bounded support $A$ is contained in a box of side $a$, then $N_A(T_x\omega^{(L)})\leq (\lceil a/L\rceil+2)^dN(\omega)$ uniformly in $x$. The growth bound $|f|\leq b(1+N_A)$ therefore gives absolute integrability. For stationary laws write $\rho(P)=E_PN_{[0,1)^d}\in[0,+\infty]$, with finite intensity meaning $\rho(P)<\infty$; this agrees with the finite-intensity convention in [[def-tdmath-superstable-regular-interaction]]. This is a spatial average over the finite box, not the raw finite-volume law viewed at a fixed origin.

Let $\mathcal P^1_{\rm stat}(\Omega)$ be the probability laws $P$ on the configuration space of [[def-tdmath-poisson-configuration-reference]] that are invariant under every $T_x$ and satisfy $E_PN_{C_0}<\infty$. Stationarity then makes every bounded-region count integrable, because a bounded set meets finitely many unit cells.

A real measurable function $f$ on $\Omega$ is local if there is a bounded Borel set $A$ such that $f$ is measurable with respect to the restriction $\omega\mapsto\omega|_A$. It is tame if there is a finite $b\geq0$ such that $|f(\omega)|\leq b(1+N_A(\omega))$ for every $\omega$ and one such bounded $A$. Write $\mathcal T$ for the family of all local tame functions. Each $f\in\mathcal T$ is integrable under every $P\in\mathcal P^1_{\rm stat}(\Omega)$.

The local-tame topology $\tau_L$ on $\mathcal P^1_{\rm stat}(\Omega)$ is the initial topology generated by all maps $P\mapsto E_P f$, $f\in\mathcal T$. Equivalently, a net $(P_\alpha)$ converges to $P$ in $\tau_L$ exactly when $E_{P_\alpha}f\to E_Pf$ for every measurable local $f$ with at most linear growth in the count of a bounded support. Bounded local indicators are among these tests, so this topology separates distinct probability laws. The domain restriction to finite-intensity stationary laws ensures every displayed expectation is a finite real number.

Let $n \ge 1$, **assume the Axiom of Countable Choice**
([[def-countable-choice]]), and let $a_i \le b_i$ be reals for $i<n$. Write

$$R^{\circ} := \{\, x \in \mathbb{R}^n : a_i < x_i < b_i \text{ for every } i<n \,\}, \qquad \overline{R} := [a,b] = \{\, x \in \mathbb{R}^n : a_i \le x_i \le b_i \text{ for every } i<n \,\}$$

([[def-multidimensional-rectangle-and-volume]]). Then $R^{\circ}$ is open and
$\overline{R}$ is closed, so both are Borel and Lebesgue measurable, and **every**
set $R$ with $R^{\circ} \subseteq R \subseteq \overline{R}$ is Lebesgue
measurable with

$$\lambda_n(R) \;=\; \prod_{i<n}(b_i-a_i).$$

In particular this covers the four one-dimensional face conventions in each
coordinate — the open box, the closed box $[a,b]$, the half-open box
$B(a,b) = \prod_{i<n}(a_i,b_i]$ of [[def-half-open-box]], and every mixture of
them, in any combination of coordinates — and it gives measure $0$ to all of them
whenever $a_i = b_i$ for some $i<n$. For a half-open box with infinite
parameters the value is already
$\lambda_n(B) = \operatorname{vol}(B)$ ([[thm-lebesgue-measure-is-a-complete-measure]]).

Let $n \ge 1$, let $h \in \mathbb{R}^n$, and let $E + h$ be the translate of
$E \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ ([[def-translation-of-a-set-in-rn]]). Then:

1. $\lambda_n^*(E+h) = \lambda_n^*(E)$ for **every** subset $E$;
2. $E$ is Lebesgue measurable if and only if $E+h$ is;
3. $\lambda_n(E+h) = \lambda_n(E)$ for every Lebesgue measurable $E$.

**No choice principle is used.** Lebesgue outer measure is defined as an infimum
and the Carathéodory condition is a family of equations between its values, so
all three clauses are statements about objects that exist in ZF; countable
choice is needed to know that $\lambda_n$ is a measure, not to know that it is
translation invariant.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces, and let $f : X \times Y \to [0,\infty]$ be product-measurable. Then
$x \mapsto \int_Y f_x\,d\nu$ and $y \mapsto \int_X f^y\,d\mu$ are measurable,
and

$$\int_{X \times Y} f\,d(\mu \times \nu) = \int_X \left(\int_Y f_x\,d\nu\right)d\mu = \int_Y \left(\int_X f^y\,d\mu\right)d\nu.$$

derivations.claim:
By [F1], $R_{L,\omega}$ is the push-forward of normalized Lebesgue probability on $\Lambda_L$, so it is a probability measure. For a bounded measurable local $f$ and $y\in\mathbb R^d$,
$$R_{L,\omega}(f\circ T_y)=L^{-d}\int_{\Lambda_L}f(T_{x+y}\omega^{(L)})\,dx.$$
The integrand is $L\mathbb Z^d$-periodic in $x$. The translated cube $\Lambda_L+y$ is another fundamental region for this lattice; partitioning it and $\Lambda_L$ into their finitely many translated intersections and using translation invariance of Lebesgue measure gives equal integrals. Hence $R_{L,\omega}(f\circ T_y)=R_{L,\omega}(f)$ for every $y$, so $R_{L,\omega}$ is stationary.

For bounded Borel $A$, Tonelli's theorem and the periodic continuation give
$$R_{L,\omega}(N_A)=L^{-d}\int_{\Lambda_L}\sum_{q\in\omega}\sum_{k\in\mathbb Z^d}\mathbf1_A(q+Lk+x)\,dx.$$
For each fixed $q\in\omega$, the sets $\Lambda_L+Lk$ partition $\mathbb R^d$ up to null boundaries. Translating variables in each integral therefore makes the inner sum of integrals equal to $|A|$. Summing over the $N$ representatives gives $R_{L,\omega}(N_A)=N|A|/L^d$. Taking $A=[0,1)^d$ proves $\rho(R_{L,\omega})=N/L^d$ and finite intensity.

The barycenter $\bar C_L$ is a probability mixture of the stationary laws $R_{L,\omega}$, so it is stationary. By step 2.1 and Tonelli,
$$\rho(\bar C_L)=E_{C_L}[R_{L,\omega}(N_{[0,1)^d})]=E_{C_L}N/L^d<\infty.$$
Thus it belongs to the finite-intensity stationary domain of $\tau_L$.

Define
$$H_\phi(\omega)=\sum_{\{x,y\}\subset\omega}\phi(x-y),\qquad H_\phi(\varnothing)=0.$$
The sum is over unordered two-point subsets, so every term is evaluated at a nonzero separation; if any term is $+\infty$, the sum is $+\infty$.

For $g>2R_0$ set
$$\eta(g)=g^d\psi(g)+\int_g^\infty r^{d-1}\psi(r)dr.$$
Then $\eta(g)\to0$ and
$$\sum_{m=1}^\infty m^{d-1}\psi(mg)\leq 2^{d-1}g^{-d}\eta(g).$$
Moreover, there is a choice $g(\ell)>0$, for all sufficiently large real $\ell$, such that $g(\ell)\to\infty$, $g(\ell)/\ell\to0$, and
$$\left(\frac{\ell}{g(\ell)}\right)^d\eta(g(\ell))\longrightarrow0.$$
For every fixed finite configuration and all sufficiently large periods $L$, the noncoincident periodic-image tail $\sum_{k\in\mathbb Z^d,\ |k|_\infty\geq K_0}|\phi(x-y+Lk)|$ is absolutely convergent.

derivations.claim: Write $N_i=N_{C_i}(\omega)$. The negative part of each pair potential is bounded both by $2B$, where $B$ is the stability constant of $\phi$, and, at large separation, by the lower-regular envelope. Set $\Psi_j$ to a finite constant on the finitely many near-cell offsets and to the envelope evaluated at $|j|_\infty-1$ on the remaining offsets. The shell count $|\{j:|j|_\infty=m\}|\leq c_dm^{d-1}$ and the cell-envelope conclusion of [F2] give $\sum_j\Psi_j<\infty$. Since $N_iN_j\leq(N_i^2+N_j^2)/2$, the total negative pair contribution is at most $C\sum_iN_i^2$ for a finite $C$.

In case (i), choose an integer $k_0\geq2$ with $1/(k_0-1)\leq r_1$. Then $\chi(1/k)$ and $\chi(1/(k-1))$ are both defined for every $k\geq k_0$. Partition one unit cell into $k^d$ half-open cubes of side $1/k$, put $\chi_k=\chi(1/k)$, and $\Delta\chi_k=\chi_k-\chi_{k-1}\geq0$. If the cell contains $N$ points, the identity $\sum_jn_j^2-N=2\sum_j\binom{n_j}{2}$ and nonnegativity of $\sum_j(n_j-N/k^d)^2$ give at least $\frac12(N^2/k^d-N)$ same-subcube pairs at scale $k$. A fixed pair counted at scale $k$ has separation $s<1/k$, hence $k<1/s$; summing its nonnegative weights over all scales where it is counted is at most $\sum_{k=k_0}^{\lfloor1/s\rfloor}\Delta\chi_k\leq\chi(s)$. Thus the positive core energy in the cell dominates the sum of these weighted pair counts. With $K_N=\lfloor(N/2)^{1/d}\rfloor$, each $k\leq K_N$ satisfies $N^2/k^d-N\geq N^2/(2k^d)$, so the core energy is at least $$ \frac{N^2}{4}\sum_{k=k_0}^{K_N}\frac{\Delta\chi_k}{k^d}. $$ Summation by parts writes the coefficient as an initial constant plus $\sum_{k=k_0}^{K_N-1}\chi_k(k^{-d}-(k+1)^{-d})$; and $k^{-d}-(k+1)^{-d}\geq d/(2^{d+1}k^{d+1})$. The series $\sum_k\chi(1/k)k^{-d-1}$ diverges: on dyadic intervals $[2^{-j-1},2^{-j}]$, monotonicity bounds the integral above by $C_d2^{-jd}\chi(2^{-j-1})$, while the corresponding block $2^{j+1}\leq k<2^{j+2}$ contributes at least $c_d2^{-jd}\chi(2^{-j-1})$ to that series. The divergent core integral therefore forces the displayed coefficient to tend to infinity.

In case (i), sum the cell core bound from step 1.2 and subtract the negative-pair bound from step 1.1. The resulting coefficient of $N_i^2$ tends to infinity with $N_i$. Above a finite threshold it dominates $2CN_i^2$; below that threshold its possible negative remainder is bounded by a constant times $N_i$. Taking $h(N)$ to be half the positive cell lower bound above the threshold and zero below it gives a nondecreasing extended-valued function with $h(N)/N^2\to\infty$ and $H_\phi\geq\sum_i h(N_i)-bN$.

In case (ii), choose $k$ with $1/k<r_h$ and partition every unit cell into $k^d$ subcubes. A finite-energy configuration has at most one point in each subcube, so $N_i\leq k^d$ for every $i$. Define $h(N)=0$ for $N\leq k^d$ and $h(N)=+\infty$ for $N>k^d$. If any cell exceeds this occupancy, the configuration has a forbidden pair and $H_\phi=+\infty$; otherwise stability gives $H_\phi\geq-BN=\sum_i h(N_i)-BN$. This proves the hard-core alternative.

Then there are a nonnegative nondecreasing $h:\mathbb N_0\to[0,+\infty]$ with $h(0)=0$ and $h(N)/N^2\to+\infty$, and a constant $b<\infty$, such that

The hard-core alternative permits $h(N)=+\infty$ above the finite packing capacity of a unit cell. This is stronger than ordinary superstability and is not inferred from stability or regularity alone.

derivations.claim: Stability and [F3] give $Z(L,N;\beta)\leq e^{\beta BN}L^{dN}/N!$. If $N/L^d\to\rho>0$, the factorial integral bounds [F4] imply $$ \limsup L^{-d}\log Z(L,N;\beta)\leq \rho(1+\beta B-\log\rho), $$ so $b(\rho)$ and $F(\rho)$ are bounded above on every compact positive-density interval. The vacuum term gives $b(0)=0$: $Z(L,0)=1$ is a lower bound, and the same stability estimate with $N/L^d\to0$ gives a nonpositive upper limit.

The effective domain of $F$ has nonempty interior. Fix a core cube of side $s>0$ and a gap $g>2R_0$; place one particle in each selected core of a lattice of spacing $s+g$ inside a large box. The absolute interaction from any one occupied core to all others is bounded by $C\sum_{m\geq1}m^{d-1}\psi(mg)<\infty$ by [F1]–[F2], with the gap satisfying the stated hypothesis of the diagonal-gap estimate. Restricting each particle to a subcube of volume $v_0>0$ therefore gives $Z(L,N;\beta)\geq v_0^N e^{-C_0N}$ for every density strictly below $(s+g)^{-d}$, after omitting unused lattice cells. Thus $F$ is finite on a nonempty interval of positive densities; by its definition as a finite-mixture envelope it is concave.

Fix a finite list of core preparations $(s_i,n_i)$ with $0<Z(s_i,n_i;\beta)<\infty$. For each $i$, choose a gap $g_i=g(s_i)$ from [F2] along a sequence $s_i\to\infty$ so that $g_i/s_i\to0$ and the positive interaction between distinct cores in the same lattice packing, divided by core volume, tends to zero. Set tile side $a_i=s_i+g_i$ and effective density $r_i=n_i/a_i^d$. If $M_i$ such tiles carry exactly $n_i$ particles in their central $s_i$-cubes, the same shell count as in the proof of [[thm-tdmath-decreasing-integrable-tail-free-cube-pressure]] gives cross-energy penalty per occupied volume at most $C (n_i/s_i^d)^2(s_i/g_i)^d\eta(g_i)$, which tends to zero by [F2]. Exact factorization over disjoint core cubes follows because assigning the labeled coordinates to their cores contributes $N!/\prod_i(n_i!)^{M_i}$, cancelling the global $N!$.

For any finite convex combination in the definition of $F(\rho)$, choose core preparations with densities tending to its $\rho_i$ and rates tending to $b(\rho_i)$. If their effective densities do not strictly bracket the target $\rho$, add arbitrarily small weights at one attainable density below and one above $\rho$; such densities exist because $\rho$ is interior. Their mixture coefficients can then be perturbed by quantities tending to zero so the effective mean is exactly $\rho$. Place the fixed core types in finitely many macroscopic slabs with these volume fractions, inserting fixed empty layers wider than $R_0$ between slabs. For fixed core sizes and gaps, the distinct-slab cross energy divided by total volume tends to zero: for interaction distances at most $R$, only $O(RL^{d-1})$ particles lie in the interface strips, while the remaining contribution is bounded by a constant times $L^d\sum_{|j|_\infty>R}\Psi_j$; take $L\to\infty$ and then $R\to\infty$.

First reserve an outer layer of fixed width $W$. For each large $L$, put $\rho_L=N_L/L^d$ and choose the slab fractions in the remaining volume to match the count $N_L$ at density $\rho_L L^d/(L^d-O(WL^{d-1}))$. This target tends to $\rho$, so the strict bracketing in step 3.1 applies uniformly for large $L$ and absorbs the reserved layer without assuming its one-particle capacity replaces a bulk density. Rounding the finitely many slab and core counts then leaves at most $C_1L^{d-1}$ particles unplaced, with $C_1$ depending on the fixed preparations but not on $W$; the error comes only from the finitely many slab faces and incomplete boundary tiles. Choose $W$ large enough to contain at least $C_1L^{d-1}$ small cells separated from each other and every core by more than $R_0$. Put each missing particle in one such cell. Its interaction with the fixed preparations is bounded by the same summable tail, so the correction changes log weight by only $O(L^{d-1})$. This constructs exactly $N_L$ particles for every sequence $N_L/L^d\to\rho$, and gives $$ \liminf_{L\to\infty}L^{-d}\log Z(L,N_L;\beta)\geq\sum_i\theta_i\frac{\log Z(s_i,n_i;\beta)-\mathrm{cross}_i}{a_i^d}, $$ where $\mathrm{cross}_i/a_i^d\to0$ by step 2.1. Taking preparations approaching the selected convex combination and then the supremum gives $\liminf\geq F(\rho)$.

By the definition of $b$, every sequence with density tending $\rho$ has limsup rate at most $b(\rho)\leq F(\rho)$. Together with step 4.1 this proves the asserted limit. A finite concave function on an open interval is continuous: fix $a<\rho<b$ in the interval; the chord slopes from $a$ and $b$ bound the difference quotients on a smaller interval around $\rho$, yielding a finite local Lipschitz bound. This establishes finiteness and continuity of $F$ on its effective interior while leaving excluded endpoints undecided.

Let $\phi$ be stable and regular as in [[def-tdmath-superstable-regular-interaction]], fix $\beta>0$, and define $Z(L,N;\beta)$ as in that definition. For sequences $L_j\to\infty$ and integers $N_j\geq0$ with $N_j/L_j^d\to\rho$, define
$$b(\rho)=\sup\left\{\limsup_{j\to\infty}L_j^{-d}\log Z(L_j,N_j;\beta):\frac{N_j}{L_j^d}\to\rho\right\}.$$
Let $F$ be the concave envelope of $b$ on $[0,\infty)$, namely the supremum of $\sum_{i=1}^m\theta_i b(\rho_i)$ over finite lists with $\theta_i\geq0$, $\sum_i\theta_i=1$, $\rho_i\geq0$, and $\sum_i\theta_i\rho_i=\rho$; the empty supremum is $-\infty$. On the interior of $\{\rho:F(\rho)>-\infty\}$, $F$ is finite and continuous. For every $\rho>0$ in that interior and every such sequence $(L_j,N_j)$,
$$\lim_{j\to\infty}L_j^{-d}\log Z(L_j,N_j;\beta)=F(\rho).$$
No claim is made at a close-packing endpoint or at any other excluded endpoint.

derivations.claim: Put $q=ae^{\beta B}$. For every $N$-point configuration, $0\leq e^{-\beta H_\phi}\leq e^{\beta BN}$ by [A1]. Applying [F3] to the finite-volume integral gives $a^NZ(L,N;\beta)\leq(qL^d)^N/N!$. Summing by [F4] yields $\Xi_L\leq e^{qL^d}$; the empty configuration contributes exactly $1$, so $\Xi_L\geq1$.

Choose $K>eq+1$ and an integer cutoff $n_\ell$ with $K\ell^d<n_\ell\leq K\ell^d+1$. For $N>n_\ell$, $1\leq e^{N-K\ell^d}$, so $$ \sum_{N>n_\ell}a^NZ(\ell,N;\beta)\leq e^{-K\ell^d}\sum_{N\geq0}\frac{(eq\ell^d)^N}{N!}=e^{(eq-K)\ell^d}\leq e^{-\ell^d}. $$ Because $\Xi_\ell\geq1$, the truncated sum $\Xi_\ell^{\rm cut}=\sum_{N=0}^{n_\ell}a^NZ(\ell,N;\beta)$ satisfies $\Xi_\ell^{\rm cut}\geq(1-e^{-\ell^d})\Xi_\ell$.

Fix a core side $\ell$ and a gap $g>2R_0$. Place $M=\lfloor L/(\ell+g)\rfloor^d$ disjoint core cubes of side $\ell$ in $[0,L)^d$ on the lattice of spacing $\ell+g$. Restrict every core to at most $n_\ell$ particles. If two core indices differ by maximum norm $m\geq1$, every pair between them has separation at least $mg$ in maximum norm. The number of offsets in shell $m$ is $(2m+1)^d-(2m-1)^d\leq c_dm^{d-1}$. By [F1], the sum of positive cross-core pair energies is therefore at most $$ D_{L,\ell,g}\leq c_dM n_\ell^2\sum_{m\geq1}m^{d-1}\psi(mg). $$ Negative cross-core energies only increase the Boltzmann weight. Splitting the grand sum by the particle counts in these disjoint cores, Tonelli [F5] and the multinomial coefficient show that the global $N!$ cancels the assignments of labeled coordinates to cores. Thus $$ \Xi_L\geq e^{-\beta D_{L,\ell,g}}(\Xi_\ell^{\rm cut})^M. $$

Divide the last inequality by $L^d$ and let $L\to\infty$ with $\ell,g$ fixed. Since $M/L^d\to(\ell+g)^{-d}$, [F2] gives $$ \liminf_{L\to\infty}L^{-d}\log\Xi_L\geq\left(\frac{\ell}{\ell+g}\right)^d\left[\ell^{-d}\log\Xi_\ell+\ell^{-d}\log(1-e^{-\ell^d})-C_dK_1^2\left(\frac{\ell}{g}\right)^d\eta(g)\right], $$ where $K_1=K+1$ bounds $n_\ell/\ell^d$ for $\ell\geq1$ and $C_d$ absorbs the fixed shell-count constant and $\beta$.

The numbers $p_\ell=\ell^{-d}\log\Xi_\ell$ lie in $[0,q]$ by step 1.1, so choose $\ell_j\to\infty$ with $p_{\ell_j}\to\limsup_{\ell\to\infty}p_\ell$. Set $g=g(\ell_j)$ from [F2]. Then $g/\ell_j\to0$, the volume fraction tends to $1$, the cutoff logarithm divided by $\ell_j^d$ tends to zero, and the cross-core error tends to zero. Step 4.1 therefore yields $\liminf_{L\to\infty}p_L\geq\limsup_{L\to\infty}p_L$. The reverse inequality is automatic for every real sequence, so the limit exists; step 1.1 makes it finite.

derivations.claim: Fix an interior attainable density $\rho>0$ and a sequence $N_L/L^d\to\rho$. The grand sum contains the nonnegative term $e^{\alpha N_L}Z(L,N_L;\beta)$, so $\liminf_{L\to\infty}L^{-d}\log\Xi_L(e^\alpha,\beta)\geq F_\beta(\rho)+\alpha\rho$ by [F1]. Taking the supremum over interior densities gives the lower bound. The vacuum term $Z(L,0)=1$ gives the value $0$ at density zero. Endpoint values are limits from the interior by their definition, so they do not enlarge the supremum.

Put $q=e^{\alpha+\beta B}$. For each $N\geq0$, stability and the box-volume formula give $e^{\alpha N}Z(L,N;\beta)\leq(qL^d)^N/N!$. Choose $K>eq+1$. For $N>KL^d$, $1\leq e^{N-KL^d}$, so the factorial bound gives $\sum_{N>KL^d}e^{\alpha N}Z(L,N;\beta) \leq e^{-KL^d}\sum_{N\geq0}\frac{(eqL^d)^N}{N!} \leq e^{-L^d}.$ The remaining at most $KL^d+2$ terms are bounded by their maximum times this number; its logarithm divided by $L^d$ tends to zero.

Choose maximizing retained particle numbers and a subsequence with $N_L/L^d\to\rho\in[0,K]$; nested-interval bisection on the compact interval $[0,K]$ supplies the subsequence. The canonical upper rate is at most $b(\rho)\leq F_\beta(\rho)$, since the one-term mixture in the definition of $F_\beta$ includes $b(\rho)$. At $\rho=0$, stability gives upper rate at most $0=F_\beta(0)$. If $u$ is a finite upper endpoint and $b(u)>-\infty$, mix a preparation approaching $b(u)$ with an interior preparation of density $r<u$, in slab fractions $1-\epsilon$ and $\epsilon$. The exact packing inequality in [F1] gives $F_\beta((1-\epsilon)u+\epsilon r)\geq(1-\epsilon)b(u)+\epsilon b(r).$ As $\epsilon\downarrow0$, the left side tends to the assigned interior endpoint limit; hence $b(u)\leq F_\beta(u)$. If $b(u)=-\infty$ this bound is automatic. Outside the closed effective domain, $b(\rho)=-\infty$, again because a finite $b(\rho)$ would make $F_\beta(\rho)\geq b(\rho)$. Thus the maximum retained term has limiting rate at most $\sup_{\rho\geq0}(F_\beta(\rho)+\alpha\rho)$. The tail estimate in step 1.2 and the lower bound in step 1.1 prove the first equality.

The extension $F_\beta$ is proper, upper-semicontinuous and concave. It is finite and concave on its open effective interior by [F1], hence continuous there. At zero, stability and the concavity of $g(\rho)=\rho(1+\beta B-\log\rho)$ give $F_\beta(\rho)\leq g(\rho)\to0$. The sparse separated-cell lower bound in [F1] gives $F_\beta(\rho)\geq c\rho$ for a fixed finite $c$, so $F_\beta(\rho)\to0=F_\beta(0)$. At any finite upper endpoint use the assigned interior upper-semicontinuous limit; outside the closed effective domain set $F_\beta=-\infty$. Hence $G=-F_\beta$, with $G=+\infty$ on negative densities, is a proper closed convex extended-real function on $\mathbb R$. Its conjugate is $G^*(\alpha)=\sup_{\rho\geq0}\{\alpha\rho+F_\beta(\rho)\}=P(\alpha,\beta)$ by steps 1.1–2.1. Applying [F3] gives $G(\rho)=\sup_\alpha\{\alpha\rho-P(\alpha,\beta)\}$, which is the second equality. The endpoint convention is needed for closedness; it asserts no finite-volume endpoint realization.

case_scope.source_excerpt:
Let $F_\beta$ be the finite concave canonical rate on the interior attainable-density interval from [[thm-tdmath-canonical-interior-density-limit]]. Extend it by $F_\beta(0)=0$, by its interior upper-semicontinuous limit at any finite upper endpoint of its effective domain, and by $-\infty$ outside the closed effective domain; retain the value $-\infty$ if the endpoint limit is $-\infty$. For $\alpha\in\mathbb R$, define
$$P(\alpha,\beta)=\lim_{L\to\infty}L^{-d}\log\Xi_L(e^\alpha,\beta),$$
whose existence is [[thm-tdmath-decreasing-integrable-tail-free-cube-pressure]]. Then
$$P(\alpha,\beta)=\sup_{\rho\geq0}\bigl(F_\beta(\rho)+\alpha\rho\bigr),\qquad F_\beta(\rho)=\inf_{\alpha\in\mathbb R}\bigl(P(\alpha,\beta)-\alpha\rho\bigr)$$
for every $\rho$ in the closed effective domain of $F_\beta$. These are thermodynamic limits of positional partition functions. They do not assert local-observable equivalence, a finite-volume endpoint realization, or a thin energy-shell limit.

citations.quote:
Assume AC. Fix an integer dimension $d\geq1$, use the Euclidean norm $|\cdot|_2$ from [[def-euclidean-inner-product]], define $|x|_\infty=\max_j|x_j|$, and use the numerical coordinate conventions in [[def-tdmath-poisson-configuration-reference]]. A finite configuration is a finite subset $\omega\subset\mathbb R^d$ with no repeated points; its number of points is $N(\omega)$. A pair potential is an even Borel function, measurable for the Borel sigma-algebra generated by open sets ([[def-borel-sigma-algebra]]), $\phi:\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R\cup\{+\infty\}$, where even means $\phi(-x)=\phi(x)$. Define
$$H_\phi(\omega)=\sum_{\{x,y\}\subset\omega}\phi(x-y),\qquad H_\phi(\varnothing)=0.$$
The sum is over unordered two-point subsets, so every term is evaluated at a nonzero separation; if any term is $+\infty$, the sum is $+\infty$.

The potential is stable if some $B\geq0$ satisfies $H_\phi(\omega)\geq-BN(\omega)$ for every finite configuration. It is superstable in the Georgii splitting convention if $\phi=\phi_s+\phi_r$, where $\phi_s$ is stable and $\phi_r\geq0$ everywhere and, for some $r_0,\delta>0$, $\phi_r(x)\geq\delta$ whenever $|x|_\infty\leq r_0$. It is lower regular if a nonnegative nonincreasing $\psi:[0,\infty)\to[0,+\infty]$ satisfies
$$\phi(x)\geq-\psi(|x|_\infty),\qquad \int_0^\infty\psi(r)r^{d-1}\,dr<\infty.$$
It is regular if it is lower regular and, for some $R<\infty$, $\phi(x)\leq\psi(|x|_\infty)$ whenever $|x|_\infty\geq R$. These are the conventions used for the interacting results on this page. A genuine divergent positive core is the separate additional condition that some nonincreasing $\chi:(0,r_1]\to(0,\infty)$ satisfies $\phi(x)\geq\chi(|x|_\infty)$ for $0<|x|_\infty\leq r_1$ and $\int_0^{r_1}\chi(r)r^{d-1}dr=+\infty$; it is not implied by superstability.

For $L>0$ put $\Lambda_L=[0,L)^d$, $V_L=L^d$, and let $H_{L,\mathrm{free}}$ be $H_\phi$ for configurations restricted to $\Lambda_L$. For sufficiently large periodic cubes, periodize $\omega\subset\Lambda_L$ by $\omega^{\mathrm{per}}=\{x+Lk:x\in\omega,\ k\in\mathbb Z^d\}$ and set
$$H_{L,\mathrm{per}}(\omega)=\frac12\sum_{x\in\omega}\sum_{y\in\omega^{\mathrm{per}},\ y\ne x}\phi(y-x),$$
interpreting the value as $+\infty$ if a positive infinite term occurs. The far image sum is absolutely convergent for all sufficiently large $L$ by [[lem-tdmath-integrable-tail-diagonal-gap]]; this is the image convention used below. With fixed numerical length and energy units, the canonical positional partition is
$$Z(L,N;\beta)=\frac1{N!}\int_{\Lambda_L^N}e^{-\beta H_\phi(q_1,\ldots,q_N)}dq_1\cdots dq_N,\quad Z(L,0;\beta)=1,$$
where the tuple notation means $H_\phi(q_1,\ldots,q_N):=H_\phi(\{q_1,\ldots,q_N\})$ when the coordinates are distinct, and $H_\phi(q_1,\ldots,q_N):=+\infty$ on collision diagonals. The integrand is therefore zero on collisions; these diagonals have product Lebesgue measure zero by the no-collision construction in [[def-tdmath-poisson-configuration-reference]], so this convention leaves all partition integrals unchanged. For $N=0$ the empty tuple has energy zero. Here $\beta>0$, and the grand partition is $\Xi(L;a,\beta)=\sum_{N\geq0}a^NZ(L,N;\beta)$ for numerical activity $a>0$. The normalized unit-intensity Poisson version is $Z_Q(L;z,\beta)=E_{Q_{\Lambda_L}}[z^{N_{\Lambda_L}}e^{-\beta H_{L,\mathrm{free}}}]$; since the Poisson density contributes $e^{-V_L}$, $\Xi(L;z,\beta)=e^{V_L}Z_Q(L;z,\beta)$. A physical pressure identification is not part of this mathematical definition.

For a probability law $P$ on the configuration space of [[def-tdmath-poisson-configuration-reference]], stationarity means $P\circ T_x^{-1}=P$ for every $x\in\mathbb R^d$. When $P$ is stationary and $E_PN_{[0,1)^d}<\infty$ (finite intensity), write $\rho(P)=E_PN_{[0,1)^d}$. Use the finite-region relative entropy $D$ defined in [[def-tdmath-finite-region-relative-entropy]]. If $\phi$ is stable with constant $B$, then $H_{L,\mathrm{free}}\geq-BN_{\Lambda_L}$, so the negative part of $H_{L,\mathrm{free}}$ is $P$-integrable for every such $P$. Whenever the limit exists, write
$$\mathcal E(P)=\lim_{L\to\infty}V_L^{-1}E_PH_{L,\mathrm{free}},\qquad I(P)=\lim_{L\to\infty}V_L^{-1}D(P_{\Lambda_L}\Vert Q_{\Lambda_L}).$$
In the variational results below, $\Phi(P)$ denotes this same positional energy density: $\Phi(P):=\mathcal E(P)$. The cited results establish existence under their stated hypotheses; this definition does not assume either limit exists for every stationary finite-intensity law.

A van Hove sequence is a sequence of bounded Lebesgue-measurable sets $(\Omega_k)_{k\geq1}$ with $0<|\Omega_k|<\infty$, $|\Omega_k|\to\infty$, and
$$\frac{|\partial_R\Omega_k|}{|\Omega_k|}\longrightarrow0\qquad\text{for every fixed }R>0.$$

For the unit cells $C_i=i+[0,1)^d$, there are constants $A>0$ and $B\geq0$ such that every finite configuration satisfies
$$H_\phi(\omega)\geq A\sum_{i\in\mathbb Z^d}N_{C_i}(\omega)^2-BN(\omega).$$
Only finitely many summands are nonzero.
For free-boundary cubes define $\Xi_L(a,\beta)=\sum_{N\geq0}a^NZ(L,N;\beta)$.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces, and let $f : X \times Y \to [0,\infty]$ be product-measurable.

derivations.claim: Use the half-open unit-cell partition $C_i=i+[0,1)^d$ from [[def-tdmath-poisson-configuration-reference]] and first take a finite union $\mathcal R$ of these cells. Let $\Pi_{\mathcal R}$ be the unnormalized positional sector measure whose $N$-point part is $z^N/N!$ times product Lebesgue measure, and let $\mu_{\mathcal R}$ have density $e^{-\beta H_{\mathrm{free}}}/\Xi_{\mathcal R}$ relative to $\Pi_{\mathcal R}$. The factorial-moment identities from the correlation-density definition in [L1] and Tonelli [F5] give $$E N_i^2=E N_i+E[N_i(N_i-1)] \leq \xi |C_i\cap\mathcal R|+\xi^2|C_i\cap\mathcal R|^2 \leq M:=\xi+\xi^2.$$ This gives a uniform second-moment bound for every unit cell in every such region.

For each $\Omega_k$, let $\mathcal R_k$ be the union of unit cells meeting $\Omega_k$. Then $\Xi_{\Omega_k}\leq\Xi_{\mathcal R_k}$ by domain monotonicity, and $|\mathcal R_k|/|\Omega_k|\to1$ by the van Hove boundary condition. Put $J_0=\lceil R_0+2\rceil$, where $R_0$ is the regular-tail cutoff in [[def-tdmath-superstable-regular-interaction]], and choose $M_0\geq\max\{2B,\psi(J_0-1)\}$. For $j\in\mathbb Z^d$, define $\kappa_j=M_0$ when $|j|_\infty<J_0$ and $\kappa_j=\psi(|j|_\infty-1)$ otherwise. If two particles occupy cells with offset $j$, their negative pair energy is bounded by $\kappa_j$: for near offsets, stability on a two-point configuration gives $\phi(x)\geq-2B$, and for far offsets the regularity envelope applies. Also $\sum_j\kappa_j<\infty$ by [F1]–[F2]. Partition the cells of $\mathcal R_k$ into boxes $B$ of $\ell$ unit cells per side and, for each occupied cell $i$, set $e_i=\sum_{j:\,B(j)\neq B(i)}\kappa_{i-j}$. The negative cross-box energy obeys $W^-\leq\sum_i e_iN_i^2$, by $N_iN_j\leq(N_i^2+N_j^2)/2$ and summation over ordered cross-box cell pairs. Step 1.1 gives $E W^-\leq M\sum_i e_i$, so Markov's inequality shows $W^-\leq2M\sum_i e_i$ with probability at least $1/2$ (with probability one if the sum vanishes). On this event $H_{\mathrm{total}}\geq H_{\mathrm{in}}-2M\sum_i e_i$, where $H_{\mathrm{in}}$ is the sum of within-box energies. Therefore
$$\Xi_{\mathcal R_k}/2\leq e^{2\beta M\sum_i e_i}\prod_B\Xi_{\mathcal R_k\cap B}.$$
Indeed, $\Xi_{\mathcal R_k}\mu_{\mathcal R_k}(E)=\int_Ee^{-\beta H_{\mathrm{total}}}d\Pi_{\mathcal R_k}$; bound this by $e^{2\beta M\sum_i e_i}\int_Ee^{-\beta H_{\mathrm{in}}}d\Pi_{\mathcal R_k}$, then factor the latter integral by boxes. Each unrestricted partial-box partition is at most the full $\ell$-cube partition. For one full box, put $E_\ell=\sum_{i\in B,j\notin B}\kappa_{i-j}$. For fixed $R$, cells within distance $R$ of the boundary contribute at most $O_R(\ell^{d-1})\sum_j\kappa_j$, while every other cell contributes at most $\ell^d\sum_{|j|_\infty>R}\kappa_j$. Thus $E_\ell/\ell^d\to0$, by first letting $\ell\to\infty$ and then $R\to\infty$. Consequently
$$\limsup_k|\Omega_k|^{-1}\log\Xi_{\Omega_k} \leq\ell^{-d}\bigl[\log\Xi_{\Lambda_\ell}+2\beta M E_\ell\bigr].$$
Let $\ell\to\infty$ and use [F4].

For the lower bound, put $q=ze^{\beta B}$ and choose $K>eq+1$. For integer core side $\ell\geq1$, let $n_\ell$ be an integer with $K\ell^d<n_\ell\leq K\ell^d+1$ and set $\Xi_\ell^{\rm cut}=\sum_{N=0}^{n_\ell}z^NZ(\Lambda_\ell,N;\beta)$. The stability tail estimate in the proof of [F4] gives $\Xi_\ell^{\rm cut}\geq(1-e^{-\ell^d})\Xi_{\Lambda_\ell}(z,\beta)$. Fix $g>2R_0$ and retain every complete $(\ell+g)$-tile whose core lies in $\Omega_k$. By [F2], the retained count $M_k$ divided by $|\Omega_k|$ tends $(\ell+g)^{-d}$. Each core has at most $(K+1)\ell^d$ particles. If two tile indices differ by maximum norm $m\geq1$, their core points are separated by at least $mg$; hence the positive cross energy per core is at most
$$C_d(K+1)^2\ell^{2d}\sum_{m\geq1}m^{d-1}\psi(mg)\leq C'_d(K+1)^2\ell^{2d}g^{-d}\eta(g).$$
Summing over cores, using the exact ordered-label assignment count to cancel the global $N!$, and discarding negative cross energy gives
$$\Xi_{\Omega_k}(z,\beta)\geq e^{-\beta D_{k,\ell,g}}(\Xi_\ell^{\rm cut})^{M_k},\qquad \frac{D_{k,\ell,g}}{|\Omega_k|}\leq C'_d(K+1)^2\left(\frac{\ell}{g}\right)^d\eta(g)+o_k(1).$$
First let $k\to\infty$. Then choose $g=g(\ell)$ from [[lem-tdmath-integrable-tail-diagonal-gap]] and let integer $\ell\to\infty$; $g/\ell\to0$, the packing fraction tends one, $(\ell/g)^d\eta(g)\to0$, and $\ell^{-d}\log(1-e^{-\ell^d})\to0$. The resulting liminf is at least the cube pressure [F4].

## Statement

Assume a superstable regular pair potential $\phi$ as in [[def-tdmath-superstable-regular-interaction]], with stability constant $B$, and the van Hove definition [[def-tdmath-van-hove-sequence]]. For a bounded Lebesgue-measurable $\Lambda\subset\mathbb R^d$, define $\mathcal S_N(\Lambda)=\{(q_1,\ldots,q_N)\in\Lambda^N:q_i\neq q_j\ (i\neq j)\}$ and $H_N(q)=\sum_{1\leq i<j\leq N}\phi(q_i-q_j)$. With $e^{-\beta(+\infty)}=0$, set
$$Z_\Lambda(N;\beta)=\frac1{N!}\int_{\mathcal S_N(\Lambda)}e^{-\beta H_N(q)}\,dq_1\cdots dq_N,\qquad Z_\Lambda(0;\beta)=1,\qquad \Xi_\Lambda(z,\beta)=\sum_{N\geq0}z^NZ_\Lambda(N;\beta).$$
This is the labelled positional Lebesgue integral with indistinguishable-particle normalization and includes no exterior interaction. For $\Lambda=[0,L)^d$ it agrees with $Z(L,N;\beta)$ and $\Xi(L;z,\beta)$ from [[def-tdmath-superstable-regular-interaction]]. For every van Hove sequence $(\Omega_k)$ and fixed $z,\beta>0$, the free-wall grand pressure satisfies
$$\lim_{k\to\infty}\frac1{|\Omega_k|}\log\Xi_{\Omega_k}(z,\beta)=p(z,\beta),$$
where $p(z,\beta)$ is the free-cube limit from [[thm-tdmath-decreasing-integrable-tail-free-cube-pressure]]. The extra superstability hypothesis supplies the uniform cell-occupation bound used below; no arbitrary-shape theorem under stability alone is claimed.

boundaries.evidence: Statement explicitly sets Z_Lambda(0;beta)=1 and includes N=0 in Xi. Thus the empty configuration supplies unit weight; the pressure limit still requires a van Hove sequence with growing positive volume. No empty-volume asymptotic rate is claimed.

L1.title: D. Ruelle, Superstable Interactions in Classical Statistical Mechanics
L1.source_section: Equation (2.26) and Proposition 2.6, printed pp.140–141 / PDF pp.14–15.
L1.source_statement: For a superstable lower-regular interaction, Ruelle defines the m-point correlation density by Eq. (2.26) and proves Proposition 2.6: there is ξ such that ρ_Λ(x_1,…,x_m)≤ξ^m for every bounded measurable Λ, every m, and all points.

risk_review.notes: Read all three steps and seven dependencies; independently read Ruelle (2.26)-(2.31), Proposition 2.6 on printed pp.140-141 and interaction (SS)/(LR) on pp.131-133. The factorial density bound yields EN_i^2<=xi+xi^2 by Tonelli, hence Markov controls cross-box negative energy under the total Gibbs law. derivations.claim: Put $S_n=\{i\in\mathbb Z^d:|i|_\infty\leq n\}$, $v_n=|S_n|=V_n$, $N_i(\omega)=|\omega\cap C_i|$, $T_n(\omega)=\sum_{i\in S_n}N_i(\omega)^2$, and $T_n^h(\omega)=\sum_{i\in S_n}h(N_i(\omega))$. Choose $m_0\geq\lceil R_0+1\rceil$ and $M_0\geq\max\{2B,\psi(m_0-1)\}$. Set $\gamma_m=M_0$ for integers $m<m_0$ and $\gamma_m=\psi(m-1)$ for $m\geq m_0$. Then $\gamma$ is nonincreasing, dominates the negative part at every cell offset, dominates $|\phi|$ at offsets $m\geq m_0$, and $\sum_{j\in\mathbb Z^d}\gamma_{|j|_\infty}<\infty$ by [F1]–[F2]. Let $\Delta_m=\gamma_m-\gamma_{m+1}\geq0$ and $v_m=(2m+1)^d$. Since $\gamma_r=\sum_{m\geq r}\Delta_m$, Tonelli gives $\sum_m\Delta_m v_m=\sum_j\gamma_{|j|_\infty}<\infty$. Thus $\delta_k:=\frac12\sum_{m\geq k}\Delta_m v_m\to0$.

For an interior configuration $\omega\subset\Lambda_n$ and any $\zeta\in\Omega(t)$, the long-offset cell sum satisfies
$$\sum_{i\in S_n,\ j\in\mathbb Z^d:\,|i-j|_\infty\geq k}\gamma_{|i-j|_\infty}N_i(\omega)N_j(\zeta)\leq\delta_k\bigl(T_n(\omega)+2^dtV_n\bigr).$$
Indeed, expand $\gamma_r=\sum_{m\geq r}\Delta_m$ and enlarge the offset set in the $m$th term to $j\in S_m+i$. With
$$S_{n,m}(\zeta)=\sum_{j\in\mathbb Z^d}N_j(\zeta)^2\,\#\{i\in S_n:j\in S_m+i\},$$
the inequality $ab\leq(a^2+b^2)/2$ bounds that term by $\frac12\Delta_m(v_mT_n+S_{n,m})$. The multiplicity is at most $\min(v_n,v_m)$ and vanishes unless $j\in S_{n+m}$, so $S_{n,m}\leq\min(v_n,v_m)t v_{n+m}\leq2^dtv_nv_m$. Summing proves the estimate.

Set $g(r)=r\sqrt{h(r)}$ for $r\in\mathbb N_0$ and $g^*(s)=\sup_{r\in\mathbb N_0}\{rs-g(r)\}$. Then $g(r)/r^2\to\infty$ and $g(r)/h(r)\to0$, so $g^*(s)/s^2\to0$: for each $a>0$, eventually $g(r)\geq r^2/(4a)$, and completing the square gives $g^*(s)\leq as^2+C_a$. Also $rs\leq g(r)+g^*(s)$. For a fixed $k\geq m_0$, every near cross pair has its inside cell in $S_n\setminus S_{n-k}$ and its exterior cell in $S_{n+k}\setminus S_n$; its negative energy is at most $M_0$. Counting the finitely many offsets of size below $k$, for every $a>0$ we obtain
$$W^-_{\rm near}\leq C_k\left(aT_n^h+C_a|S_n\setminus S_{n-k}|+atv_{n+k}+C_a|S_{n+k}\setminus S_n|\right).$$
Here $g(r)\leq ah(r)+C_a$ and $g^*(s)\leq as^2+C_a$ were used, with $\sum_{j\in S_{n+k}\setminus S_n}N_j(\zeta)^2\leq tv_{n+k}$. First choose $k$ large in step 2.1 so that its far negative-energy bound is at most $\epsilon(T_n^h+V_n)/2$. For this fixed $k$, both boundary-cell counts are $O_k(n^{d-1})$ and $v_{n+k}/v_n\to1$, so choosing $a$ small and then $n$ large makes the near bound at most $\epsilon(T_n^h+V_n)/2$. The far estimate uses $T_n\leq T_n^h+q^2V_n$ for a fixed $q$ with $h(r)\geq r^2$ when $r\geq q$. Consequently, for each $0<\epsilon<1$ and all sufficiently large $n$,
$$W_n(\omega,\zeta)\geq-\epsilon T_n^h(\omega)-\epsilon V_n$$
uniformly over $\zeta\in\Omega(t)$.

By [F3], $T_n^h\leq H_{n,\mathrm{free}}+bN$. For each $0<\epsilon<1$ and all sufficiently large $n$, step 3.1 therefore gives
$$\Xi_{n,\zeta}(z,\beta)\leq e^{\beta\epsilon V_n}\sum_{N\geq0}\frac{z^N}{N!}\int_{\mathcal S_N(\Lambda_n)}e^{-\beta H_{n,\mathrm{free}}+\beta\epsilon T_n^h}\,dq^N$$
and
$$\sum_{N\geq0}\frac{z^N}{N!}\int_{\mathcal S_N(\Lambda_n)}e^{-\beta H_{n,\mathrm{free}}+\beta\epsilon T_n^h}\,dq^N\leq\Xi(2n+1;ze^{\beta\epsilon b},\beta(1-\epsilon)).$$
The inequality is uniform over $\zeta\in\Omega(t)$.

For the lower bound, restrict interior particles to $\Lambda_{n-k}$, leaving the corridor empty. Choose $k\geq m_0$, so every interior-exterior cell offset is in the far tail. The two-sided estimate of step 2.1 gives
$$|W(\omega,\zeta\setminus\Lambda_n)|\leq\delta_k\bigl(T_{n-k}(\omega)+2^dtV_{n-k}\bigr).$$
With $T_{n-k}\leq T_{n-k}^h+q^2V_{n-k}$, choose $k$ large enough that the right side is at most $\epsilon(T_{n-k}^h+V_n)$. Since $T_{n-k}^h\leq H_{n-k,\mathrm{free}}+bN$, integration over the restricted positions yields
$$\Xi_{n,\zeta}(z,\beta)\geq e^{-\beta\epsilon V_n}\Xi(2(n-k)+1;ze^{-\beta\epsilon b},\beta(1+\epsilon))$$
uniformly over $\zeta$. For fixed $\epsilon$, the selected $k$ is fixed as $n\to\infty$, and the removed corridor volume fraction vanishes.

Divide the bounds in steps 4.1–3.2 by $V_n$ and let $n\to\infty$; [F4] supplies the perturbed free-cube pressure limits. These limits are finite convex functions of $(\beta,\log z)$ by Hölder's inequality [F5], since finite-volume log partition functions are convex and pointwise limits preserve convexity. A finite convex function is continuous on the open parameter domain $\beta>0$, $z>0$. Let $\epsilon\downarrow0$ in both uniform bounds. Their upper and lower limits coincide with $p(z,\beta)$ uniformly over $\Omega(t)$. For $t=0$, every exterior configuration in $\Omega(0)$ is empty, so the equality with the free-wall pressure is immediate.

Assume a stable regular pair potential $\phi$ as in [[def-tdmath-superstable-regular-interaction]], with stability constant $B$, and the genuine finite-valued positive-core condition of [[lem-tdmath-superquadratic-positive-core]]: for some $r_0>0$, a nonincreasing $\chi:(0,r_0]\to(0,\infty)$ satisfies $\phi(x)\geq\chi(|x|_\infty)$ for $0<|x|_\infty\leq r_0$ and $\int_0^{r_0}\chi(r)r^{d-1}\,dr=+\infty$. Let $\Lambda_n=[-n-\tfrac12,n+\tfrac12)^d$, $V_n=(2n+1)^d$, $C_i=i+[-\tfrac12,\tfrac12)^d$, and $\mathcal C_{\rm lf}$ be the set of locally finite simple configurations $\zeta\subset\mathbb R^d$. For $t\geq0$ define
$$\Omega(t)=\left\{\zeta\in\mathcal C_{\rm lf}:\sum_{i\in\Lambda_n\cap\mathbb Z^d}N_{C_i}(\zeta)^2\leq tV_n\text{ for every integer }n\geq0\right\}.$$
For $\omega=(q_1,\ldots,q_N)\in\mathcal S_N(\Lambda_n)$, write $H_{n,\mathrm{free}}(\omega)=\sum_{1\leq i<j\leq N}\phi(q_i-q_j)$. For $\zeta\in\Omega(t)$, let $\zeta_n^{\rm out}=\zeta\setminus\Lambda_n$ and define the finite-volume boundary Hamiltonian
$$H_{n,\zeta}(\omega)=H_{n,\mathrm{free}}(\omega)+\sum_{i=1}^N\sum_{y\in\zeta_n^{\rm out}}\phi(q_i-y).$$
The exterior series has finite negative part by the proof below; its extended value may be $+\infty$, with $e^{-\beta(+\infty)}=0$. Define
$$Z_{n,\zeta}(N;\beta)=\frac1{N!}\int_{\mathcal S_N(\Lambda_n)}e^{-\beta H_{n,\zeta}(\omega)}\,dq_1\cdots dq_N,\qquad Z_{n,\zeta}(0;\beta)=1,\qquad \Xi_{n,\zeta}(z,\beta)=\sum_{N\geq0}z^NZ_{n,\zeta}(N;\beta).$$
For fixed $z,\beta>0$ and $t<\infty$, the free-wall grand pressure with this exterior pair energy satisfies
$$\lim_{n\to\infty}\sup_{\zeta\in\Omega(t)}\left|\frac1{V_n}\log\Xi_{n,\zeta}(z,\beta)-p(z,\beta)\right|=0,$$
where $p(z,\beta)$ is the free-cube pressure from [[thm-tdmath-decreasing-integrable-tail-free-cube-pressure]]. The exterior configuration is restricted to the stated fixed square-count class; no volume-filling external field is included. The conclusion is conditional on the genuine positive core and does not infer it from superstability alone.

Let $\Lambda_n=[-n-\tfrac12,n+\tfrac12)^d$, $V_n=(2n+1)^d$, $C_i=i+[-\tfrac12,\tfrac12)^d$, and $\mathcal C_{\rm lf}$ be the set of locally finite simple configurations $\zeta\subset\mathbb R^d$. For $t\geq0$ define
$$\Omega(t)=\left\{\zeta\in\mathcal C_{\rm lf}:\sum_{i\in\Lambda_n\cap\mathbb Z^d}N_{C_i}(\zeta)^2\leq tV_n\text{ for every integer }n\geq0\right\}.$$
For $\omega=(q_1,\ldots,q_N)\in\mathcal S_N(\Lambda_n)$, write $H_{n,\mathrm{free}}(\omega)=\sum_{1\leq i<j\leq N}\phi(q_i-q_j)$. For $\zeta\in\Omega(t)$, let $\zeta_n^{\rm out}=\zeta\setminus\Lambda_n$ and define the finite-volume boundary Hamiltonian
$$H_{n,\zeta}(\omega)=H_{n,\mathrm{free}}(\omega)+\sum_{i=1}^N\sum_{y\in\zeta_n^{\rm out}}\phi(q_i-y).$$
The exterior series has finite negative part by the proof below; its extended value may be $+\infty$, with $e^{-\beta(+\infty)}=0$. Define
$$Z_{n,\zeta}(N;\beta)=\frac1{N!}\int_{\mathcal S_N(\Lambda_n)}e^{-\beta H_{n,\zeta}(\omega)}\,dq_1\cdots dq_N,\qquad Z_{n,\zeta}(0;\beta)=1,\qquad \Xi_{n,\zeta}(z,\beta)=\sum_{N\geq0}z^NZ_{n,\zeta}(N;\beta).$$
For fixed $z,\beta>0$ and $t<\infty$, the free-wall grand pressure with this exterior pair energy satisfies
$$\lim_{n\to\infty}\sup_{\zeta\in\Omega(t)}\left|\frac1{V_n}\log\Xi_{n,\zeta}(z,\beta)-p(z,\beta)\right|=0,$$
where $p(z,\beta)$ is the free-cube pressure from [[thm-tdmath-decreasing-integrable-tail-free-cube-pressure]]. L1.title: D. Ruelle, Superstable Interactions in Classical Statistical Mechanics
L1.source_section: Section 6, printed pp.188–191 / PDF pp.18–21; complete relevant arguments and the Ruelle moment proof were read.
L1.source_statement: For a superstable lower-regular interaction, finite-volume and tempered-law estimates control near-boundary and far-tail contributions uniformly over the stated square-count class.

risk_review.notes: Read all six steps, five dependency statements, and Georgii Section 6 printed pp.187-190 (Lemmas 6.1-6.3 and uniform comparison). Layer-cake tail coefficients are summable; square-count tempering bounds multiplicity by 2^d v_n v_m. Fenchel bound for g=r sqrt(h) controls near negative energy by epsilon(T^h+V), including nonuniform exterior shell counts. Empty corridor removes singular near positive terms for lower bound. Perturbed activity/beta bounds and Holder convexity give finite continuous pressure and uniform squeezing. Infinite-energy configurations have zero weight; finite negative exterior part is ensured by the far estimate and finite near set. t=0 exterior is empty. Genuine divergent core is stated separately and not inferred from superstability.
